title: Pressure
question: What is pressure?

principle.name: Pressure
principle.formulaNote: pressure = force ÷ area, in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). In a liquid or gas at rest it also grows with depth: P = ρ g h.
principle.idea: Pressure is how concentrated a push is: the same force squeezed onto a small area presses much harder than when it is spread over a big one. Air and water press too, harder the deeper you go.
principle.discovered: 1643 · Evangelista Torricelli's barometer; 1648 · Pascal's Puy de Dôme

examples.title: Stiletto vs elephant
examples.text: A 60 kg person on a 1 cm² heel presses the floor at about 5.9 MPa. A 4,000 kg elephant on four broad feet manages only about 80 kPa, some 75 times less.

examples.title: A car tyre’s contact patch
examples.text: Each wheel of a family car carries about 3.3 kN. At 2.2 bar the tyre flattens until the patch touching the road is about 150 cm², palm-sized: load ÷ area ≈ tyre pressure.

examples.title: Hard bicycle tyres
examples.text: A road bike’s narrow tyres run at 5–7 bar, so each touches the road with only about 9–11 cm². That small, firm patch is why they roll so easily.

examples.title: Tank pressure and the RO pump
examples.text: A rooftop tank 10 m up gives a tap only about 1 bar (P = ρgh). An RO membrane needs about 5 bar, so the purifier carries its own booster pump.

examples.title: The geyser’s safety valve
examples.text: Heated water expands in a sealed tank and the pressure climbs fast. A relief valve lets a little out at 6–8 bar, far above anything a rooftop tank can supply.

examples.title: Blood pressure at heart height
examples.text: 120/80 mmHg is the pressure at heart level. Blood is a liquid column, so a cuff on the ankle reads almost 100 mmHg more; that’s why the arm is rested at heart height.

examples.title: Popping ears
examples.text: Dive 2 m or fly down to land and the pressure outside the eardrum changes while the middle ear stays behind. Swallowing lets air through the Eustachian tube to even it out.

examples.title: Boiling on demand in an AC
examples.text: Water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm, 88 °C in Leh and 120 °C in a pressure cooker. An AC uses the same rule: its refrigerant boils cold at low pressure and condenses hot at high pressure.

examples.title: Magdeburg hemispheres
examples.text: In 1654 von Guericke pumped the air out of two copper half-spheres. The outside air pushed them together with about 20 kN, more than teams of horses could pull apart.

examples.title: The bottom of the Mariana Trench
examples.text: Nearly 11 km down the sea presses at about 1,086 bar, over a tonne on every square centimetre. Trieste reached it in 1960 inside a steel ball 12.7 cm thick.

hook: Why does a stiletto dent a floor an elephant wouldn’t, why is a dam thickest at the bottom, and why does dal cook faster under a whistle? Squash sand, cut a tomato, lie on nails, fill a dam, pump out Magdeburg’s hemispheres and dive the Mariana Trench.

explainer.title: Force on an area
explainer.text: Pressure is force divided by area, P = F ÷ A, measured in pascals: one newton on one square metre. Press a plate into sand and halve its area: the pressure doubles and it sinks deeper. A brick on its end presses three times harder than lying flat, and a stiletto heel beats an elephant by about 75 times. The units board shows every pressure in Pa, kPa, bar, atm, psi and mmHg.

explainer.title: Sharp and wide
explainer.text: A sharp knife’s edge turns 10 N into megapascals and splits a tomato; a blunt one squashes it. Snowshoes, a bed of a thousand nails and fat low-pressure tractor tyres spread weight to keep pressure low. A tyre’s contact patch is about load ÷ pressure: palm-sized for a car at 2.2 bar, stamp-sized for a bike at 6 bar.

explainer.title: Deeper means harder
explainer.text: Under a liquid, P = ρ g h: every 10 m of water adds about 1 bar. A rooftop tank gives the ground floor about 1 bar, far short of an RO pump’s 5. Bhakra Dam’s 226 m of water press at 2.2 MPa at the base. Unequalised ears hurt a metre or two down, and blood pressure is highest at your ankles.

explainer.title: An ocean of air
explainer.text: Air presses at about 101 kPa at sea level. Pump air out of Magdeburg hemispheres and 20 kN clamps them. A straw lifts juice by lowering the pressure in your mouth. Pressure falls with height, to 65 kPa in Leh and a third on Everest, so water boils cooler; a pressure cooker’s 82 g whistle holds 1 bar extra and boils at 120 °C. A mercury barometer stands 760 mm tall.

explainer.title: Myths and extremes
explainer.text: Gauges show pressure above the air: a “flat” tyre still holds 1 atm. Suction never pulls, the outside air pushes, so a suction cup fails on Mars. The Mariana Trench presses at about 1,086 bar. And vessels of any shape filled to the same depth have the same pressure at the bottom: Stevin’s hydrostatic paradox.

concepts.def: Force divided by the area it acts on, P = F ÷ A.
The SI unit of pressure: one newton per square metre. 1 bar = 100,000 Pa; 1 atm = 101,325 Pa.
Pressure in a still liquid from the weight above: P = ρ g h. About 1 bar per 10 m of water.
The weight of the air above pressing on everything, about 101 kPa at sea level and less as you climb.
Gauges read the pressure above the surrounding air; absolute pressure adds the air’s 1 atm back.
An instrument that measures air pressure, first a column of mercury about 760 mm tall (Torricelli, 1643).
The temperature where water’s vapour pressure matches the pressure around it: lower up mountains, higher in a pressure cooker.
Pressure at the bottom of a liquid depends only on depth, not on the shape or size of the container.
